bib.title: Rephrasing the Web: A Recipe for Compute and Data-Efficient Language Modeling
bib.venue: preprint (arXiv:2401.16380v1 [cs.CL], 29 Jan 2024; PDF does not print a venue)

read.skipped: References skimmed only; Table 7 and Fig 12-13 values not in text (plots / ratio list).

question: Can rephrasing noisy web documents with an off-the-shelf instruction-tuned LLM, and pre-training on a mix of real and rephrased text, make LLM pre-training cheaper in compute and data?
hypothesis: Rephrased synthetic data has higher utility than real data alone because it adds style diversity matching downstream evaluation and is higher quality than web scrapes; synthetic data cannot add new knowledge, only speed up learning.
contributions: WRAP: rephrase web documents in specific styles with a frozen instruction-tuned model and pre-train on a 1:1 real/synthetic mix
~3x pre-training speed-up on C4, Pile perplexity and 13-task zero-shot gains
Analysis of rephrase style, combination of styles, rephraser quality, augmentation baselines, and leakage

method.summary: A frozen Mistral-7B instruction-tuned model rewrites C4 paragraphs (max 300 tokens each) into Medium (Wikipedia-like) and Q/A styles; decoder-only GPT-style models (128M, 350M, 1.3B) are pre-trained from scratch on a 1:1 mix of real C4 and synthetic rephrases, and compared on Pile perplexity (21 domains) and 13 zero-shot tasks against real-data-only baselines.
method.task: next-token pre-training of decoder-only LMs on real plus synthetic rephrased web text

datasets.name: C4
datasets.size: about 170B tokens full; half C4 about 85B
datasets.split: Half C4 (85B) and Full C4 (170B) real-token budgets; 35B real subset for 150B-token runs
datasets.source: Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus, derived from CommonCrawl
datasets.preprocessing: rephrased with Mistral-7B; paraphrases cleaned with NLTK sentence split to drop lead-in phrases such as 'Here's a paraphrase'; residual error rate under 0.1% by manual inspection (App. B)

datasets.name: RefinedWeb
datasets.split: first 3050 files for 300B-token run; first 1650 files for multi-epoch

datasets.name: The Pile (validation, 21 sub-domains)
datasets.size: first 10,000 documents per domain, split into pieces of max 1024 tokens
datasets.preprocessing: Europarl excluded in one place (20 subsets in App. A.2; 21 stated in main text)

datasets.name: 13 zero-shot tasks (LM Evaluation Harness)
datasets.source: General: ARC-E, BoolQ, Winogrande, PIQA, HellaSwag, TruthfulQA, OBQA, LogiQA-2; Specialized: ARC-C, SciQ, PubMedQA, MathQA, MMLU

other.also tried: Qwen-1.8B-chat, Vicuna-13B-chat-v1.3, fine-tuned T5-base (1 epoch on Vicuna rephrase pairs)
other.throughput: 3M tokens per hour on a single A100 with vLLM

models.name: TinyLlama
models.architecture: trained 3 epochs on 1T tokens of SlimPajama and StarCoder

other.inconsistency: text says 1 Trillion tokens (3 epochs) in Sec 5.2 and '3 Trillion tokens' in Sec 7.1

training.objective: next-token cross-entropy (language modeling) over C4 union synthetic rephrases
training.steps: 300k for XL models unless otherwise specified (150B-token runs halve the steps)
training.compute: 300B tokens about 256 GPU days, about 6k GPU hours; generating 85B synthetic tokens about 25K GPU hours
training.seeds: WRAP results in Tables 1-2 averaged over 3 runs; Table 12 single seed 1234

other.real tokens: 'Real Tok.' counts web tokens only, since one document can be rephrased several times

inference.samples: one rephrase per document inferred from 1:1 ratio
inference.prompting: chat template 'A chat between a curious user and an artificial intelligence assistant...' then USER instruction per style (App. G)

parameters.real:synthetic: 1:1; combined-style variants 1:1 (two C4 copies) and 1:2 (one C4)

metrics.name: Pile perplexity
metrics.definition: macro token-level perplexity P=exp(min(20, L/T)); weighted average over domains by Table 7 ratios

metrics.name: zero-shot accuracy
metrics.definition: LM Evaluation Harness, 8 General Understanding and 5 Specialized Knowledge tasks, averaged

metrics.name: few-shot leaderboard (App. F)
metrics.definition: ARC-C 25-shot, HellaSwag 10, MMLU 5, TruthfulQA 5, Winogrande 5, GSM8k 5

eval.protocol: Pile perplexity on first 10k docs per domain; zero-shot via harness; WRAP zero-shot averaged over 3 runs; no significance test; C4-validation perplexity deliberately not used.

prompts.text: A chat between a curious user and an artificial intelligence assistant. The assistant gives helpful, detailed, and polite answers to the questions. USER: For the following paragraph give me a diverse paraphrase of the same in high quality English language as in sentences on Wikipedia:

A chat between a curious user and an artificial intelligence assistant. The assistant gives helpful, detailed, and polite answers to the questions. USER: Convert the following paragraph into a conversational format with multiple tags of "Question:" followed by "Answer:":

A chat between a curious user and an artificial intelligence assistant. The assistant gives helpful, detailed, and polite answers to the questions. USER: For the following paragraph give me a paraphrase of the same using a very small vocabulary and extremely simple sentences that a toddler will understand:

A chat between a curious user and an artificial intelligence assistant. The assistant gives helpful, detailed, and polite answers to the questions. USER: For the following paragraph give me a paraphrase of the same using very terse and abstruse language that only an erudite scholar will understand. Replace simple words and phrases with rare and complex ones:

evidence.quote: 24 layers, 16 attention heads, and a hidden dimension size of 2048

results.claim: WRAP on C4 speeds up pre-training about 3x (abstract); Fig 1a shows ~3x faster to equal average zero-shot accuracy.
results.setup: 1.3B GPT models, WRAP-85B vs C4-85B/C4-170B/RW-300B, avg zero-shot accuracy vs tokens seen
results.quote: First, we show that using WRAP on the C4 dataset, which is naturally noisy, speeds up pre-training by ∼3×.

results.claim: At equal compute, WRAP improves Pile perplexity by more than 10% on average and zero-shot accuracy across 13 tasks by more than 2%.
results.setup: C4, mixed real+synthetic; Pile sub-domains; 13 zero-shot tasks
results.quote: At the same pre-training compute budget, it improves perplexity by more than 10% on average
results.note: Introduction and Data Complexity paragraph state about 50% perplexity reduction on the Pile instead (different comparison: vs real data alone).

results.claim: Average Pile perplexity falls about 50% versus models trained on real data alone.
results.quote: Overall, on an average of multiple subsets of the Pile, our models improve perplexity by 50% over models trained on real data alone.
results.note: Abstract says 'more than 10%' at equal compute; Fig 2 compares C4+QA-85B with C4-85B and C4-170B.

results.claim: Synthetic+C4 (85B real tokens) averages 49.4% on General Understanding vs 47.4% for Half C4 (85B).
results.setup: ~1.3B, 85B real tokens, WRAP averaged over 3 runs; style not named in Table 1 (Fig 2 and Table 12 use C4+QA)
results.quote: models trained on synthetic data combined with the C4 dataset (Synthetic+C4) exhibit an overall higher average performance of 49.4% as compared to those trained solely on the real C4 dataset with a 85B token split, which scored an average of 47.4%.

results.claim: On Specialized Knowledge tasks WRAP gives no new knowledge: Synthetic+C4 (85B) avg 45.5 vs Full C4 (170B) 43.5, comparable to Pythia and TinyLlama (45.6).
results.quote: The key message from the results in Table 2 is that synthetic data can not impart ‘new knowledge’.
results.table: Table 2, rows Synthetic+C4 (85B) and TinyLlama (1T), column Avg (45.5 and 45.6)

results.claim: TruthfulQA is the largest single gain: Synthetic (85B) scores 44.0%, and adding C4 drops it to 40.5%.
results.note: Text says 40.5%, Table 1 prints 40.6 for Synthetic+C4; text says 'by 4%'.

results.claim: Dropping real C4 (synthetic only) raises Pile perplexity on many domains, notably PhilPapers and Gutenberg; only shown in Fig 3, no numbers.
results.setup: 1.3B, 150B tokens, 35B real subset; Med-35B and QA-35B vs C4+Med/QA-35B
results.quote: On domains such as Philpapers and Gutenberg, we observe that dropping real C4 text from the pre-training data, and training on synthetic documents alone drops performance significantly (increase in perplexity).

results.claim: Synthetic-only vs with real zero-shot, General avg: Med 45.8 vs Med+C4 46.7; QA 48.2 vs QA+C4 48.4. Specialized avg: Med 42.7 vs Med+C4 40.8 (reversed); QA 43.8 vs QA+C4 45.0.
results.quote: adding real data helps improve model performance when pre-training on ‘Medium’ or ‘Wikipedia-style’ paraphrases.
results.table: Table 3 (General) and Table 4 (Specialized), rows Med-35B, Med+C4-35B, QA-35B, QA+C4-35B, column Avg

results.claim: Combining Medium and Q/A styles does not beat Q/A+C4 on zero-shot (General avg 47.5 and 48.0 vs 48.4) but slightly improves average Pile perplexity.
results.quote: Overall, we note that there is a small improvement on the average perplexity on the Pile by combining multiple styles.
results.table: Table 6, rows Combined-1:1-35B, Combined-1:2-35B, column Avg

results.claim: Rephraser quality: Qwen-1.8B and Mistral-7B rephrases give lower perplexity than Vicuna-13B; fine-tuned T5-base is significantly worse but still beats real C4 alone.
results.quote: We find that pre-training on data generated by smaller re-phrase models like Qwen-1.8B and Mistral-7B achieve lower perplexity than Vicuna 13B (Figure 5).

results.claim: Synonym replacement and random deletion augmentations are significantly worse than real+rephrased data.
results.quote: the models trained on augmented data perform significantly worse than those trained on combinations of real and synthetic data.

results.claim: An oracle choosing the best synthetic style per Pile domain would improve perplexity by 16%; no single style is best.
results.quote: an oracle that selects the best synthetic style across all domains will improve perplexity by 16%

results.claim: Generating 85B synthetic tokens with Mistral-7B costs about 25K GPU hours; training one 1.3B model on 300B tokens is about 6k GPU hours; a 13B model about 30K.
results.setup: vLLM on A100, 3M tokens/hour; 64 A100 at 0.5M tokens/s
results.quote: Generating 85B tokens (as in our work) accounts for about 25K GPU hours.

results.claim: At 350M/75B tokens, adding QA rephrases lifts General avg 42.7 (C4-75B) -> 44.1 (QA+C4-18B) and Specialized avg 38.2 (C4-60B) -> 41.0.
results.quote: We also show an increase of 1.5% across general understanding language tasks, and roughly 3% on specialized knowledge tasks
results.table: Table 9 row QA+C4-18B Avg 44.1; Table 8 row QA+C4-15B Avg 41.0

results.claim: Few-shot leaderboard avg: QA+C4-85B (300K) 37.2 and QA+C4-100B (350K) 37.5 vs C4 35.5, Falcon-RW 37.1, Pythia-1.4b 35.0; single seed.
results.quote: Evaluation is done on a single seed (1234).

limits: Cost of generation still large and needs strong LMs (Sec 8)
Enforcing diversity in generated data is unresolved; content diversity of paraphrase models not assessed (Sec 7.2)
Only C4 rephrased; models 128M-1.3B; no post-training or larger scale; larger models may benefit from training longer (Sec 7.1)
Perplexity evaluated on Pile, not C4, because mixed training costs under 1 perplexity on C4 validation
Medium vs QA vs other styles mostly shown as plots (Fig 3-7); per-domain numbers not in text
Which style the headline 'Synthetic' rows use is not stated in Tables 1-2; Fig 2 and Table 12 indicate QA
WRAP zero-shot averaged over 3 runs but baselines' seeds not stated; no significance tests
No code or data release stated in text

terms.definition: Web Rephrase Augmented Pre-training: an off-the-shelf instruction-tuned model prompted to paraphrase web documents in specific styles to jointly pre-train on real and synthetic rephrases
number of tokens of web data available for pre-training, used as comparison metric because one document can be rephrased many times

lineage.note: WRAP avoids generating from scratch: smaller rephraser, uses web diversity
repeating more than 4 epochs diminishing returns
cited as harm of synthetic data; WRAP not tested for it
